articles.title: Five signs an MVP has competing sources of truth
articles.meta_description: How seed-stage MVPs accumulate silent data conflicts — five signals that competing sources of truth will block safe scaling.
articles.audience: Founders and engineering leads at seed–Series B startups
articles.problem: The product ships features, but teams disagree on what a user, balance, or order actually is — and fixes get slower as you grow.
articles.author: AmirSaber Sharifi

sections.heading: 1. The same noun maps to different schemas
sections.content: If “user,” “wallet,” or “position” has different field sets across services, you already have multiple truths. The UI may look coherent while APIs answer incompatible questions.

sections.heading: 2. Read paths disagree after common flows
sections.content: A deposit, trade, or onboarding step completes successfully, but dashboards, emails, and support tools show different states. That is not a caching bug — it is unowned entity lifecycle.

sections.heading: 3. Migrations are avoided because no one owns the model
sections.content: Teams add nullable columns and shadow tables instead of consolidating. Each shortcut preserves a local source of truth and pushes reconciliation to the next team.

sections.heading: 4. Event logs and primary tables tell different stories
sections.content: When the event stream says one thing and the row users see says another, you lack a defined write model. Replays and audits become arguments, not procedures.

sections.heading: 5. New features require “which system is right?” meetings
sections.content: If every cross-cutting feature starts with a meeting to pick the authoritative store, delivery cost is already compounding. The MVP is working around its own data model.

articles.title: What investors should examine before funding fintech architecture
articles.meta_description: Technical due diligence questions for fintech investments — ledger boundaries, reconciliation, and security posture beyond the pitch deck.
articles.audience: Investors and operating partners evaluating fintech and digital-asset companies
articles.problem: Architecture risk rarely appears in pitch decks, but it determines whether a funded company can scale compliance, custody, and settlement without a rewrite.
articles.author: AmirSaber Sharifi

sections.heading: Ledger and balance boundaries
sections.content: Ask where balances are authoritative, how pending vs. settled funds are represented, and what happens when a provider webhook arrives twice. Double-entry without clear ownership is still a single point of failure.

sections.heading: Reconciliation and exception handling
sections.content: Production fintech breaks at the edges: partial settlements, chargebacks, chain reorganizations, stale quotes. Look for automated reconciliation, idempotent ingestion, and operator runbooks — not manual spreadsheets.

sections.heading: Identity, authorization, and audit trails
sections.content: Map how customer identity ties to account actions, who can move money, and whether every material action is attributable. Gaps here become regulatory and fraud incidents after growth.

sections.heading: Third-party and chain dependency posture
sections.content: Understand failover when a banking partner, indexer, or RPC endpoint degrades. Healthy architectures degrade gracefully; fragile ones hide provider outages behind incorrect user state.

sections.heading: Security debt that compounds after PMF
sections.content: MVP shortcuts — shared secrets, broad service accounts, missing encryption context — are cheap early and expensive once traffic and compliance scope grow. Ask what was deferred and what blocks enterprise or licensing paths.
